comparison: Both evaluate background/established knowledge claims (C10-C23, C115). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED noting these are established facts with appropriate citations. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, confirming these foundational claims were not challenged.

Both address ribosome biogenesis and ribosomal protein claims (C57-C65, C92-C93). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with comprehensive experimental evidence. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising critical concerns about ribosome biogenesis assessment, requesting quantification of reduced 18S rRNA, validation of Rpl5 results with multiple siRNAs, and effects of silencing other RPs.

Both evaluate Mdm2-Mdm4 interaction and Mdm4 degradation (C51-C52, C66-C68, C101-C103). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong experimental evidence. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising critical concern about Figure 4F not clearly supporting that reduced heterodimer formation is solely due to decreased Mdm4 levels, suggesting Rps27L loss may also affect binding affinity.

Both evaluate tumorigenesis and genomic instability claims (C5-C9, C79-C82, C86, C108-C114). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, finding results 'especially interesting' but raising critical concerns about mechanism—whether genomic instability could be due to selective pressure against p53 upstream regulators rather than direct Rps27L effect, requesting assessment of p53 levels/activity in MEFs.

Both evaluate tissue distribution of Mdm2/Mdm4 changes (C69-C70). Both mark SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this demonstrates p53-independent regulation. Peer review accepted without challenge, supporting generalizability beyond hematopoietic tissues.

Both evaluate hematopoietic phenotype and p53-dependence (C3-C4, C24-C37, C71-C77, C87-C90). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with multiple lines of evidence including rescue experiments. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, explicitly stating authors 'convincingly show' defects are p53-dependent and apoptotically related, with no concerns raised.

Both address Mdm2 protein stability mechanism (C97-C100). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with time-course and protein stability data. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanism showing Rps27l negatively regulates Mdm2 protein stability with convincing temporal sequence evidence.

Both evaluate temporal sequence of molecular events (C53-C54). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED showing sequential changes in both Trp53+/+ and Trp53-/- MEFs. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, not challenging this data which helped address mechanistic sequence concerns.

Both evaluate interpretations about Rps27L function (C94-C96). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting interpretations are well-supported by totality of evidence. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, questioning whether defining Rps27L as p53 inhibitor is valid, asking whether Rps27L overexpression suppresses p53 and whether it normally prohibits other RPs from stabilizing Mdm2.

Both address p53 stabilization mechanism (C47-C48, C55-C56). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with ubiquitylation assays and protein stability data. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, accepting evidence of reduced p53 ubiquitylation, extended half-life, and post-translational mechanism without concerns.

Both evaluate p53 rescue experiments (C71-C77, C89-C90). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong Kaplan-Meier, flow cytometry, and transplantation data. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, explicitly accepting rescue experiments as demonstrating causality with no concerns raised about core phenotypic findings.

Both address p53 pathway activation in MEFs (C85). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of broader genomic instability evaluation. Peer review marks SUPPORTED, noting this data was specifically requested to address whether genomic instability could be independent of p53 loss.

Both evaluate tumor suppression requiring functional p53 (C78). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with survival analysis. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED without challenge, supporting the model that Rps27l's tumor suppressive function requires at least one functional p53 allele.

Both evaluate limited role of Rps27l in genomic stability with normal p53 (C84). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical tests. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED without challenge, critical for supporting claim about limited role when p53 is normal.

Both evaluate overall mechanistic model (C116-C121). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting model is consistent with data and prior work. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, finding model interesting but raising concerns about specific mechanistic details including Mdm2-Mdm4 binding affinity and requesting inclusion of Rpl11 in model.

Both address Mdm2 stabilization (C45-C48). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with cycloheximide chase and ubiquitylation assays. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, accepting protein half-life extension and reduced self-ubiquitylation data without challenge.

Both evaluate genomic instability mechanism under p53 haploinsufficiency (C111-C114). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with genotype-specific aneuploidy effects. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about whether genomic instability is direct or due to selective pressure, requesting assessment of p53 levels/activity in MEFs.

Both address model elements related to genomic stability (C120-C121). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of mechanistic interpretation. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN as part of overall model evaluation, requesting validation of mechanistic details.

Both evaluate p53 induction specificity to ribosomal stress (C43-C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with stress response characterization. Peer review also marks SUPPORTED, not raising concerns about differential responses to various stresses supporting ribosomal stress mechanism.

Both address ribosomal stress and p53 activation convergence (C1, C91). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with converging evidence from multiple approaches. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about ribosome biogenesis assessment and requesting validation of ribosomal protein effects.

Both evaluate p53 accumulation in tissues (C38-C42). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with immunostaining and immunoblotting across tissues. Peer review marks SUPPORTED as part of broader acceptance of p53-dependent phenotype without specific concerns about tissue p53 levels.

Both address enhanced RP-Mdm2 binding (C117). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of converging mechanistic evidence. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN as part of overall model evaluation, requesting validation of mechanistic details and effects of other RPs.

Both evaluate p53-independent Mdm2 regulation (C50). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with dose-dependent regulation in p53-null cells. Peer review marks SUPPORTED as part of accepted Mdm2 stabilization mechanism.

Both address Mdm4 degradation contributing to p53 activation (C2). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with multiple experimental approaches. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about whether reduced heterodimer formation is solely due to decreased Mdm4 levels.

Both evaluate mechanistic interpretation of Mdm2-Mdm4 heterodimer function (C104). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, consistent with cited literature. Peer review marks SUPPORTED for p53 ubiquitylation mechanism but raised concerns about heterodimer binding affinity in separate result.

Both address sequential mechanistic events (C100). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of converging evidence. Peer review marks SUPPORTED, accepting temporal sequence showing Mdm2 elevation preceding Mdm4 depletion and p53 accumulation.

Both evaluate Trp53 dosage effects (C83). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with qPCR and immunoblotting. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN as part of broader concerns about genomic instability mechanism, though this specific data point was not directly challenged.

Both address clinical relevance of RPS27L expression (C115). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting external validation from patient data. Peer review marks SUPPORTED as established background fact without challenge.
